# References {#refs background-color="#f0674d"}

Search, download, check. Four jobs, one prompt each.

## Pick one

```{=html}
<div class="menu" style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;">
  <div class="pick">
    <a class="card" href="#/search"><b>Search</b><span>One specific question, or every paper since 1995</span></a>
    <a class="card" href="#/download"><b>Papers in the folder</b><span>Download what it can, a DOI for the rest. One rule, once.</span></a>
  </div>
  <div class="pick">
```

## This is in the literature right now

- An audit of 2.5 million biomedical papers found fabricated references in **1 in
  277** papers in early 2026, up from 1 in 2,828 in 2023. (A *Lancet* letter; its
  method has been questioned.)
- In my own field: a 2026 paper in *Structural Equation Modeling* cites Foldnes &
  Grønneberg (2024). The DOI resolves to a 2022 **"Editorial acknowledgement"**.
  The paper reports simulation results for methods from a source that does not exist.

> The models got better. The practice didn't.

## Search: one specific question {#search}

In fields I know well, questions like this keep turning up important papers I
didn't know existed:

::: {.prompt}
What's similar to Hjort–Glad density estimation with a parametric start? Other kernel
estimators with something that could count as a parametric start, also on domains
other than the real line? Do any outperform it? Download the papers into literature/,
and give me the DOI for any you can't get.
:::

[Hjort and Glad (1995) is a density estimator. Notice how specific the question is.]{.small .muted}

*"Papers on density estimation"* gets you the textbook. A specific question gets you
the paper you missed.

## Exercise: ask yours

1. Take the idea at the heart of your paper.
2. Ask one specific question about it:

::: {.prompt}
What's similar to [your idea, in one exact sentence]? Has anyone built something
like it? Does it beat [the usual approach]? Download the papers into literature/,
and give me the DOI for any you can't get.
:::

3. Anything you didn't know? Tell your neighbour.
4. For contrast: *"Papers on [your topic]?"* Which answer is better?

## Deep: when you need everything

A different request: you're **finalizing**, not exploring.

::: {.prompt}
I need every method since 1995 related to Hjort–Glad: working papers too, and other
names for the same idea. A table: paper, what it does, how it relates. Take your time.
:::

- For the related-work section, the grant application, the referee response.
- Slow, and it eats your usage limit. Start it, then get coffee.

## Keep the papers in the folder {#download}

Asking for that every time? Make it a rule in the project file, once:

::: {.prompt}
Add to the project file: papers go in literature/. Whenever we need one, download it
there if you can get it. If you can't, give me the DOI so I can.
:::

- It reads the paper, not its memory of it. And never hunts for it twice.
- Catching up? *"Do that for every paper in my reference list."*
- Paywall, or SSRN (blocks agents)? Your browser, then *"Move it into literature/."*

## DOI check {#doi}

::: {.prompt}
Check every entry in the reference list. Does the DOI resolve to this exact
paper: same title, authors and year? Make a table: OK, wrong paper, no DOI, not found.
:::

- Then check three yourself: paste the DOI after `doi.org/`.
- Practice file: a messy `.bib` with six planted traps (handout, section 8).

## Claim check {#claims}

The one nobody does: **does the cited paper say what it's cited for?**

::: {.prompt}
Take each citation in the introduction. Read the cited paper in literature/ and check
whether it supports the sentence it is cited for. Quote the passage. Mark each:
supports, partly, doesn't, not in the folder.
:::

- **Papers not in the folder yet?** *"Take three citations from the introduction,
  download the cited papers into literature/, then check each one."*
- Run it on your own draft before you submit.

## Round-up

- Anything wrong in your paper's reference list?
- A citation that doesn't say what it's cited for?

> A polished bibliography is not evidence of a correct bibliography.
